1:
The qualified verdict on the king is where the comment begins. Henry sets out the two halves of it together: he worshipped the true God, kept the temple service going and countenanced religion in his kingdom, yet did it with no serious piety or devotion of his own and no zeal for the exercises of religion, being no enemy to it but a cool and indifferent friend. He finds the type common in his own day, men who do what is good but not with the heart. Wesley puts the same judgement in a sentence, that the man was not an enemy to religion but a cool and indifferent friend, not of serious piety, since his heart was not whole with God. Clarke reduces it to the arc of the reign, that he began well and soon became an idolater, and points forward to the verses where that happens.

The execution of the murderers is read as justice with a limit. Henry grants that the assassins may have meant to avenge the death of the prophet killed in the previous reign, and refuses to let that justify them, since they were not the appointed avengers but presumptuously took God's work out of his hands; so the king did what became him in calling them to account, while forbidding the putting of their children to death for their fathers' sin. Ellicott works the same verse textually, noting that it coincides almost exactly with the parallel in Kings, that the literal sense is that their sons he put not to death but acted according to what is written in the law in the book of Moses, and that the reference is evidently to the command in Deuteronomy, which the other book repeats more exactly than this one; on the closing clause he observes that the Hebrew runs, each for his own sin shall they be put to death, where Kings has the singular. On the previous verse he renders the establishing of the kingdom as the confirming of the sovereignty or power to him, and cites the Latin to the same effect.

The muster that follows is noticed for what the numbers show. Henry counts the three hundred thousand men of Judah and Benjamin fit for war against the forces of Jehoshaphat some fifty or sixty years earlier, which were four times as many, and draws the inference that sin weakens a people, diminishing them and dispiriting them and lessening both their number and their figure. He treats the hiring of a hundred thousand Israelites as the king's attempt to make up with money what his own kingdom lacked in men, and judges that had he consulted any prophet beforehand, or merely considered how little any of his ancestors had got by their alliances with Israel, he would not have had the thing to undo again; rashness, he says, makes work for repentance. Clarke lays out the whole chapter in advance as a scheme of events, the reign begun well, the murderers slain and their children spared, the army reviewed and remodelled, the hired troops dismissed on a prophet's expostulation and greatly offended at it, the Edomite victory and the prisoners thrown from the rock, the ravaging of the cities of Judah by the dismissed men, the idolatry, the prophet threatened into silence, and the challenge that ends in defeat.
5:
The hired troops and the prophet's veto take up most of the comment. Ellicott notes that the number mustered falls immensely below the forces of Jehoshaphat and is not much more than half that of Asa, and allows the high figures of this book to be suspicious in general while finding a relative propriety here, since the country had suffered much in the interval; Keil and Delitzsch call the same total relatively small and gloss the muster as a census of those liable to service from twenty years old and upward. Ellicott values the hundred talents at about forty thousand pounds of his own money, reckoning four hundred to the talent. Clarke quotes the Targum on the prophet's reason, that the word of the Lord is not the helper of the Israelites nor of the kingdom of that tribe. Henry makes the reason practical as well as religious, that troops with whom God was not could not be depended on to do service, and draws the rule Wesley states in the same words, that it is comfortable to employ those who may be hoped to have an interest in heaven and dangerous to associate with those from whom the Lord has departed.

One verse of the prophet's answer is read two opposite ways. Gill takes the permission as irony: if the king will not be advised, let him take them along, exert all his courage and use his military skill, and mark the issue. Wesley says the same in a phrase, that it is an ironical concession like bidding a man go and prosper. Ellicott will not have it so, holding that a negative has dropped out of the text before the clause about falling, so that the prophet's sense is, venture on the expedition by thyself with a good courage, and God will not let thee stumble before the foe; the following clause he renders, for there is strength in God, to help and to make to stumble. Keil and Delitzsch read the charge as a call to go alone and show himself valiant.

The obedience and its cost are then weighed, and the cost comes twice. Henry sets the objection about the money beside the answer to it, that men often plead against their duty that they are afraid of losing by it, and that a firm belief of God's all-sufficiency to make up what we lose in his service makes his yoke easy. Gill hears the objection as spoken with some concern, the king being loath to lose so much money and knowing there was no demanding it back. Ellicott glosses the dismissal plainly, that the troop was sent to its own place in a heat of anger, and judges the anger natural, since the treatment seemed to indicate distrust of their honour and robbed them of the possible fruits of victory; Wesley gives both grounds, the disgrace of the rejection and the disappointment of the spoil, and suggests the hundred talents had probably gone to their officers only, to raise the men. On the massacre of the prisoners Ellicott identifies the rock as Sela, the Edomite capital known to later ages as Petra, and allows the savage treatment to be credible in view of the well-known atrocities of ancient warfare though Kings does not mention it; Henry records the same thing as certainly very severe and says we are not told what provocation there was for it. On the raid that followed, Ellicott suspects the name Samaria to be corrupt, since otherwise the mercenaries must have gone home first and then set out again by order of the northern king; Henry and Wesley both read it as a chastisement of the border cities of Judah for the idolatries they had caught from Israel, so that the men who had corrupted them became a plague to them.
14:
The absurdity of the idolatry is the first thing every voice marks. Henry calls it egregious folly and draws the contrast with a later king who at least worshipped the gods of those who had conquered him, where this one worshipped the gods of a people he had himself beaten, who could not protect their own worshippers; he asks what the king saw in them to tempt him, and suggests that for the barbarous inhumanity of the massacre he was given up to an idolatry as ridiculous as it was wicked. Gill makes the point by what the king failed to do, that instead of returning thanks to God for the victory and giving him the glory of it he brought home the conquered gods. Keil and Delitzsch describe the act plainly, that on his return from smiting the Edomites he brought the images of the sons of Mount Seir with him and set them up as gods, giving them religious adoration. Clarke supplies the Targum, which renders the phrase as the idols of the children of Gebal.

Ellicott surrounds the act with what is known of the custom and the gods. He notes that the Assyrian inscriptions often refer to carrying off the idols of conquered countries, Esarhaddon recording that he restored the gods of a king of Arabia at that prince's entreaty, and Assurbanipal that he recovered an image carried off by an Elamite sovereign sixteen hundred and thirty-five years before. He guesses at the king's motive, that he may have wished to win the favour of these gods and so keep his hold on what was reckoned their own territory, and names the likely candidates from inscriptions and royal names, Hadad, Kosh, who appears in two Edomite kings' names, and Moloch, whom a name recorded by Sennacherib shows to have been worshipped in Edom.

Whether the report can stand beside the older account is then raised twice. Keil and Delitzsch note that the statement is not found in the parallel chapter of Kings, and report the opinion that it may rest on no definite tradition but be the application to a particular case of a principle generally found at work in the history. Ellicott puts the sharper form of the objection, that a scholar of his day held it to contradict the verdict in Kings, and concedes that the chronicler does portray this king in a darker light than the older account, while answering that this proves only the independence of the two. On the reproof itself Henry observes that God sent to convince and reclaim the king before he sent to destroy him, and that the prophet reasoned very mildly, asking why he had sought the favour of gods which could not deliver their own people, from which Henry draws the rule that men who duly considered the inability of the things they run to when they forsake God would not be such enemies to themselves. On the king's answer Gill grants that the prophet was no member of the privy council but insists he was appointed a counsellor by the King of kings. Henry reads the three moves of the reply, the taunt that a man had usurped a counsellor's place, the silencing, and the threat, and notes that the threat seems to remind the prophet of the one killed in the previous reign, so that in menacing this one the king makes himself guilty of both deaths. Wesley hears in it the complacency of a secure sinner who values himself on having silenced his monitors, and answers that it is a plain indication he is marked out for ruin, since those deaf to reproof are ripening fast for destruction. Ellicott catches the wordplay that closes the exchange, the prophet taking up the king's own word about counsel and implying his own part in a counsel higher than the royal one.
17:
Whose advice the king took is the first question. Gill answers it bluntly, not of God nor of his prophets but of some of his nobles like himself. Wesley asks the same question and answers it the same way, that the counsel was about the injury the Israelites had done and how it should be repaired, and that it is good to take advice but it should be of those who are fit to advise us. Henry presses the irony that the prophet was not made of the king's counsel, so the king consulted statesmen who would flatter him and bid him go up and prosper, and lays down that those who will not take advice from the word of God will justly be left to the bad advice of men who counsel them to their destruction. Ellicott renders the challenge itself, let us look one another in the face, as combatants do, and notes that the counsel taken was a different thing altogether from the counsel the prophet would have tendered.

The fable of the thistle and the cedar is given its sting by one voice and its text by another. Clarke reports the Targum's addition after the fable, which turns the parable into a direct charge: thus hast thou done when thou didst send to me and lead up a hundred thousand strong warriors of Israel for a hundred talents of silver, and then wouldst not permit them to go with thee to war but sent them back greatly enraged, so that they spread over the country and cut off three thousand and brought back much spoil. Ellicott works the next verse word by word, noting that thou sayest or thou thinkest is added here, that the word rendered Lo may be a corruption of the word for smiting, giving thou hast indeed smitten, and that where this book has a verb meaning to get glory, used so only here, Kings has be honoured and abide at home, the difference being one of vowel points and perhaps due to a copyist. Ellicott marks the explanation that follows as the chronicler's own addition, accounting for the infatuation by the divine predetermination of events. Henry states the same thought as a principle, that the king's imprudence was made the punishment of his impiety, God leaving him to himself to act foolishly so that he and his people might be delivered to their enemies because they had forsaken him for the gods of Edom. Henry finds the whole episode a verification of two proverbs, that a man's pride will bring him low and goes before his destruction, and that he who goes out hastily to strive will not know what to do in the end when his neighbour has put him to shame.
22: The defeat, the plunder of the temple and the murder close the chapter. Ellicott carries the textual work through to the end: the Syriac and Arabic omit the verse on Judah being put to the worse, several Hebrew manuscripts give Ahaziah where our text has Jehoahaz, the corner gate appears here as the gate that turneth, which would need a word to say which way it turns, the verb he took has dropped out in an omission old enough to appear in the Greek, and the closing formula blends this book usual wording with the one customary in Kings. On the treasure Clarke and Wesley agree with him that the mention of Obed-edom reflects the custody of the sacred collections allotted to that family, Clarke citing the earlier book for the allotment of the house of collections to his descendants and Ellicott adding that the clause is the chronicler own but probably drawn from an ancient document, the name belonging to a Levitical clan. Clarke supplies the Targum on the first and last acts, the first when the king walked in the fear of the Lord and the last when he departed from the right way, and gives the political reading of the conspiracy, that the king became unpopular once the battle was lost, Jerusalem dismantled and the royal treasures seized, so that the last years of the reign were embittered and he sought safety at Lachish in vain, the man who forsook the Lord being forsaken by every friend. Ellicott takes the dating clause as asserting a connection rather than fixing a time, calling attention to the fulfilment of the prophet's sentence, and Henry reads it the same way, that from the time the king departed from the Lord the hearts of his subjects departed from him. Keil and Delitzsch end on the burial place, where the text reads city of Judah against the city of David named everywhere else as the burial place and given by all the old versions, and explain the slip as a copying error caused by the Judah that follows; Ellicott calls it a transcriber's mistake in the same terms. Ellicott notes two further shifts in the verse on the plunder, that the Latin gives the closing verb a transitive form and so makes the king carry all the things enumerated back to Samaria, where the Syriac supplies instead that he took the silver. Henry opens his account of the end with the observation that never was a poor prince more violently pursued by his own subjects.
